title: Tanager Aero edge rollforward & TF notes (draft)
content:
Context:
Tanager Aero is a regional aviation maintenance provider looking to deploy Redwood privately in their primary operations data center (hangar campus). Primary constraints: intermittent connectivity to cloud (satellite link), strict physical cooling constraints in hangar racks, and FIPS-ish KMS requirement (customer uses a vendor HSM with PKCS#11). This doc is a working rollforward/playbook + Terraform module notes for their on-prem rollout and upgrade strategy.

Goals: (what customer expects)
- Stable inference for checklists and maintenance assistant workloads with p99 latency <= 450ms for assistant prompts (median 150–220ms).
- Predictable monthly unit cost for committed capacity (Reserved nodes).
- Capability to perform safe upgrades with quick rollback while offline (air-gapped).
- Secure key management using customer HSM and audit logs forwarded to their SIEM.

High-level recommended topology (edge):
- Control plane: Private control plane deployed as a small HA pair in customer VPC segment; connectivity back to Redwood control plane limited to heartbeat-only via a TLS tunnel over satellite with buffering.
- Serving plane: 3 identical rack nodes (compute pool), each node: 2x NVIDIA A40 (or A30 depending on procurement), 512GB RAM, NVMe for KV-cache and local artifacts, 2x 10Gb NICs bonded, Ubuntu 22.04.
- Storage: local NVMe + nightly encrypted snapshots copied to an on-site NFS-backed archival cluster.
- Networking: internal BGP/routing with dedicated VLAN for inference traffic, no public ingress.
- KMS: PKCS#11 connector to vendor HSM in a separate security VLAN.

Sizing rationale (workload data provided by customer):
- Target steady state: 60 concurrent interactive sessions (chat+tooling), average request = 800 input tokens + 400 generated tokens per session per minute during peak bursts.
- Model candidate: open-llm-65B quantized (4-bit mixed). Measured average per-token throughput on a single A40 = ~400 tokens/sec (in our benchmarking for 512-seqlen batched runtime).
- Effective tokens/sec needed (system level): 60 sessions * 400 tokens = 24,000 tokens/min => 400 tokens/sec sustained.
- Accounting for batching inefficiencies and KV warmups, apply 1.8x headroom => target 720 tokens/sec sustained.
- Node capacity estimate: 2x A40 per node ~ 800 tokens/sec (with our mixed-quant kernels). So 3 nodes provide ~2400 tokens/sec headroom and allow redundancy + maintenance windows.
- Recommendation: start with 3 nodes (2 serving + 1 warm standby for rolling upgrades). If customer opts for cheaper A30s, increase node count to 4 to preserve headroom.

TF module and infra notes (practical constraints for air-gapped environment):
- Module layout: modules/*
  - modules/edge-node (compute + local disk layout + nvme formatting)
  - modules/networking (vlan, static routes, firewall rules)
  - modules/kms-connector (pkcs11 connector install + systemd service)
  - modules/artifact-distribution (local registry + signature verification)
  - modules/redwood-runtime (systemd + docker-compose/k8s manifests depending on node profile)

- Important TF decisions:
  1) Avoid external provider dependencies during apply: use local-exec to copy pre-baked artifacts from an approved internal artifact server. No remote module sources at apply time.
  2) Use static IP allocation and explicit resource naming (no random suffixes) — makes rollforward/rollback easier when control plane is semi-offline.
  3) Keep mutable secrets out of state by referencing HSM tokens at runtime instead of storing keys in TF state. The TF module should accept a HSM slot id and certificate thumbprint only.
  4) Version pin all module releases and store a signed module tarball in the customer's artifact registry.

Upgrade / rollforward playbook (air-gapped friendly):
- Prereqs before any upgrade:
  - Ensure on-site artifact registry contains new runtime artifacts and they are signed and fingerprinted in the upgrade ticket.
  - Confirm snapshot of NVMe attached volumes (local encrypted copy) and an exported copy to archival NFS.
  - Confirm HSM operator has unsealed the HSM and that PKCS#11 agent is running on every node.
  - Verify smoke endpoints on the standby node are passing (health-checks).

- Stepwise upgrade plan (minor runtime or model weight upgrade):
  1) Drain node C (standby): redirect new requests away, keep existing KV cache warm if possible.
  2) Apply TF change to update runtime artifact version for node C only. Use offline TF plan files checked into the release branch.
  3) Deploy artifacts to node C from local registry and perform smoke tests (start with a single low-QPS synthetic script that validates expected tokens/sec and model hash).
  4) Promote node C to serving for 10% of traffic (canary) for 2 hours; watch latency, error rate, and token cost.
  5) If metrics OK, sequentially repeat for node B, then node A. If any canary fails, revert node to previous artifact and re-run rollback.

- Rollback steps (fast path):
  - Re-apply TF module pointing at previous signed artifact (pre-stored). Because IPs and names are static, node identity is preserved and rollback is quick.
  - If model weights are incompatible with cache layout, purge local KV cache after rollback before bringing node back to serving.

Operational considerations & gotchas:
- Cooling constraint: racks experience temperature spikes during long retrain/inference runs. Add node-level CPU throttling for maintenance jobs and stagger batch rebuilds to limit thermal events.
- Disk wear: heavy NVMe cache usage requires monitoring; include SMART exports to central SIEM with alert when TBW > 70% of rated.
- Network flaps with satellite link: control plane heartbeats should be tolerant for 15–30 minutes of connectivity loss; avoid any automatic full-cluster failover that would trigger re-sharding.
- KMS latency: PKCS#11 calls are slower — cache unwraps locally for session lifetime when allowed by policy to avoid per-request HSM round-trips.

Open questions for customer (action items):
- Which GPU SKU will procurement finalize (A40 vs A30 vs H100)? Procurement choice changes node count and cooling needs.
- Do you require FIPS 140-2 certification and how broadly do we need to integrate HSM audit logs into your SIEM?
- What is acceptable canary exposure windows (2 hours suggested) and what SLO breach tolerance do you accept during upgrades?
- Will the site operations team want a documented physical cutover checklist for power/cooling in the rack (we should co-author one).

Notes for follow-up TF tasks (short tickets):
- TF-1: Add a module variable allow_offline_apply = true and add local artifact path vars.
- TF-2: Add outputs for node_identity and pkcs11_slot to avoid storing raw secrets.
- TF-3: Bake module tarball, sign with infra GPG key, upload to on-site registry; add acceptance test that verifies fingerprint.

Appendix: quick audit checklist before go-live:
- Node health: all nodes pass full health-check and SLO synthetic (p95 < 300ms).
- Snapshots: latest local encrypted snapshot present + off-site archival copy verified.
- HSM: PKCS#11 agent registered and test-signing succeeds.
- TF: Plan file for cutover verified by a second engineer and stored in release folder.

TL;DR recommendation: provision 3-node serving cluster with 2x A40 per node, static IP naming, pre-baked signed artifacts in an on-site registry, and a staged canary-based rollforward procedure. This balances headroom, cooling constraints, and rollback speed in an air-gapped-ish environment.

Publisher notes: draft — this is an internal playbook for the solutions and infra teams. Next steps: align with Tanager ops, get procurement GPU SKU, and schedule an on-site dry-run.
